samf-junior-2005-r1-02.title: Count the shift
samf-junior-2005-r1-02.body:
Each ordinary year moves a date one weekday forward; a year that contains 29 February between the two dates moves it two. From 16 June 2004 to 16 June 2010 there are $6$ years and one leap day (29 February 2008). The shift is $6+1=7$ days, which is a whole number of weeks. So 16 June 2010 is again a Wednesday.

**Answer: (C) Wednesday**

samf-junior-2005-r1-03.title: Find the magic sum
samf-junior-2005-r1-03.body:
The middle column is $14+10+6=30$, so every line adds to $30$. Top right: $30-9-14=7$. Bottom right (the diagonal $9,10,\_$): $30-9-10=11$. The right column is $7+x+11=30$, so $x=12$.

**Answer: (D) 12**

samf-junior-2005-r1-04.title: Find the number
samf-junior-2005-r1-04.body:
The number is $60$. Three-quarters of $60$ is $45$.

**Answer: (D) 45**

samf-junior-2005-r1-04.title: Use fractions
samf-junior-2005-r1-04.body:
Half is $30$, so a quarter is $15$ and three-quarters is $45$.

**Answer: (D) 45**

samf-junior-2005-r1-06.title: Rectangle minus the notch
samf-junior-2005-r1-06.body:
Complete the figure to a $10\times12$ rectangle. The diagonal cuts it in two halves of area $60$. The shaded region is the upper-right half with a small square cut off at the corner. That square has side $10-6=4$, so area $16$. Shaded area $=60-16=44$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: (B) 44**

samf-junior-2005-r1-07.title: Make the numbers as equal as possible
samf-junior-2005-r1-07.body:
A product with a fixed sum is greatest when the numbers are as equal as possible. $28=9+9+10$, giving $9\times9\times10=810$. Moving a unit between the numbers never helps: e.g. $8,10,10$ gives $800$ and $9,8,11$ gives $792$.

**Answer: (D) 810**

samf-junior-2005-r1-08.title: Angles round a point
samf-junior-2005-r1-08.body:
Each interior angle of a regular pentagon is $\frac{(5-2)\cdot180^\circ}{5}=108^\circ$. Three pentagons meet at the point, so $3\times108^\circ+a=360^\circ$, giving $a=36^\circ$.

**Answer: (A) $36^\circ$**

samf-junior-2005-r1-09.title: Factors of 483
samf-junior-2005-r1-09.body:
Both $\square$ and $\triangle$ divide $503-20=483=3\cdot7\cdot23$, and each exceeds $20$ (the remainder). The divisors of $483$ above $20$ are $21,23,69,161,483$. Taking $\square=21$ and $\triangle=23$ gives $\square\times\triangle=483$. Then $493=483+10$ leaves remainder $10$. (Any other pair has a product larger than $493$, which would leave remainder $493$, not among the choices.)

**Answer: (C) 10**

samf-junior-2005-r1-10.title: Split into 12 triangles
samf-junior-2005-r1-10.body:
Draw all the diagonals parallel to the sides to divide the hexagon into $12$ congruent triangles. The shaded triangle is made of $4$ of them, so it is one third of the hexagon. The hexagon has area $3\times36=108$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: (B) 108**

samf-junior-2005-r1-12.title: Angle chase
samf-junior-2005-r1-12.body:
The ticks show $DB=DC$ and $DA=DC$ in the picture. As $DB=DC$ and $\angle B=30^\circ$, $\angle C_1=30^\circ$, so $\angle D_1=120^\circ$ and $\angle D_2=60^\circ$. Triangle $ACD$ has $DA=DC$ and an apex angle $60^\circ$, so it is equilateral. Hence $AC=DC=DB=70$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 70**

samf-junior-2005-r1-13.title: Match the letters
samf-junior-2005-r1-13.body:
$T$ is in all three words and $1$ is in all three codes, so $T=1$. $A$ is only in SAT and $5$ only in $154$, so $A=5$. $N$ is only in TEN and $2$ only in $321$, so $N=2$. Then SAT gives $S=4$, and TEN gives $E=3$. So $SENT=4\,3\,2\,1$.

**Answer: (E) 4 3 2 1**

samf-junior-2005-r1-14.title: Use the volume
samf-junior-2005-r1-14.body:
Let the edges be $l,b,h$ with face areas $bh=24$, $lh=40$ and $lbh=240$. Then $l=\frac{240}{24}=10$, $b=\frac{240}{40}=6$ and the face $C$ has area $lb=60$.

**Answer: (C) 60**

samf-junior-2005-r1-15.title: Find one square
samf-junior-2005-r1-15.body:
Each square has perimeter $4x$, so six squares give $24x=72$ and $x=3$. The rectangle is $3\times2$ squares: $9\times6=54$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: (A) 54**

samf-junior-2005-r1-16.title: Work column by column
samf-junior-2005-r1-16.body:
Units: $c+b=a$ or $a+10$. Tens: $b+c$ plus a carry gives $4$ (possibly with a carry). Hundreds: $2a$ plus a carry equals $c$ with no carry out.

If there were no carry from the units, then $b+c=a\le9$ and the tens digit would be $b+c=a=4$, so $c=2a=8>a$, impossible. So the units produce a carry: $b+c=a+10$. The tens column is then $a+10+1=a+11$, which must end in $4$, so $a=3$ and there is a carry into the hundreds. Hundreds: $c=2\cdot3+1=7$. Then $b=a+10-c=6$. Check: $367+376=743$. So $a+b+c=16$.

**Answer: (E) 16**

samf-junior-2005-r1-16.title: Trial and improvement
samf-junior-2005-r1-16.body:
Since $c\approx2a$ we try $a=1,2,3,\dots$ with $c=2a$ or $2a+1$. Only $a=3,c=7,b=6$ works: $367+376=743$.

**Answer: (E) 16**

samf-junior-2005-r1-17.title: Algebra
samf-junior-2005-r1-17.body:
The number is $10(y+3)+y=11y+30$ and the digit sum is $2y+3$. Then $11y+30=7(2y+3)+3=14y+24$, so $3y=6$, $y=2$, $x=5$ and the number is $52$ with digit sum $7$. Check: $52=7\times7+3$.

**Answer: (D) 7**

samf-junior-2005-r1-17.title: Try the numbers
samf-junior-2005-r1-17.body:
The possible numbers are $30,41,52,63,74,85,96$. Dividing by the digit sum: $30\div3=10$, $41\div5=8$ r1, $52\div7=7$ r3 ✓.

**Answer: (D) 7**

samf-junior-2005-r1-18.title: Count by pairs
samf-junior-2005-r1-18.body:
Every triangle has its apex at the top vertex. Its sides along the apex are two of the $5$ lines through the apex: $\binom52=10$ choices. Its base lies on one of the $3$ horizontal lines (the base and the two cross lines): $3$ choices. Each choice gives a triangle: $10\times3=30$.

**Answer: (B) 30**

samf-junior-2005-r1-19.title: Triangular numbers
samf-junior-2005-r1-19.body:
Row $n$ ends with the triangular number $\frac{n(n+1)}2$. $\frac{24\cdot25}2=300$ and $\frac{25\cdot26}2=325$. So row $25$ runs from $301$ to $325$, and $320$ is the $320-300=20$th number in it.

**Answer: (E) 25 ; 20**

samf-junior-2005-r1-20.title: Check each player
samf-junior-2005-r1-20.body:
The only possible twin pairs are lady and brother, or son and daughter. In each case the best player is the same age as the worst player, so can be the twin only if they are the same person, and then the sexes would not be opposite.

- Lady worst: her twin is her brother, and the best player must be the same age as the lady; only her twin (the brother) qualifies, so the best player is the twin himself -- not of opposite sex to himself. Impossible.
- Daughter worst: her twin is the son; the best player of the same age as the daughter can only be the son (the same as the twin), or the brother. The brother is male like the son, so not opposite. Impossible.
- Son worst: twin is the daughter, best is the brother (same age as the son is possible) and he is of the opposite sex to the daughter. Possible.
- Brother worst: twin is the lady, best is the son (same age as the brother) of opposite sex to the lady. Possible.

So the lady and the daughter cannot be the worst player.

**Answer: (D) lady and daughter only**
